extracted_by: hand, T-0311 — the Democrat read, February 1834
note: Vol. I No. 13. Two buildings enter the town in this issue and both are dated to the week: a LIVERY STABLE opened at the Point, and a SMOKE HOUSE fitted up by D. Elston & Co. on 15 February. The county's records move house as well — the Clerk of the Circuit and County Courts is removed to the building one door west of Col. Owen's — and W. Kimball's store is set at the corner of South Water and Clark for the first time in the month.

claims.notes: A LIVERY STABLE OPENS AT THE POINT, and it is a building this reconstruction does not have. A livery is not a shed: it stalls saddle horses and houses single-horse carriages, it is worked day AND night, and it keeps horses by the day or the week — so it needs stalls, a carriage floor, a yard and a man sleeping on the premises. THE PLACEMENT IS THE PAPER'S OWN WORD AND NOTHING MORE. 'At the Point' is how this town names the forks, and the corpus already carries Wolf Point landings and frontages there; the placement is recorded `relative` on that anchor because the phrase is a location the paper expects readers to walk to, but WHICH point frontage — the west bank, the north bank, or the tongue between them — is not stated and is not inferred. The keeper's surname prints 'EPERSON' with the M dropped and is read E[m]erson; it is not identified with any Emerson elsewhere in the corpus. Running again unchanged in 1834-02-25, so the stable is open for at least a fortnight.

business.trade: provision curers and soap and candle makers

claims.notes: A SMOKE HOUSE, FITTED UP AND DATED — 15 February 1834. This is a small industrial structure with a form the model can actually draw: a smoke house is close-boarded, low, chimneyless or nearly so, and stands clear of what it could set alight, which is why it is a separate building rather than a room. The same firm runs the Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory on the other side of this issue (c010), so Elston is assembling a small works — tallow, ashes, soap, candles, and now cured meat — and the smoke house belongs with it. 'Fitted up' is the paper's phrase and is read as an existing structure adapted rather than a new frame raised; the distinction is left as the print makes it. NO SITE IS GIVEN. Elston's works are known to have stood on the North Branch but this notice does not say so, so the placement is `none` and the structure is unplaced.

claims.notes: BOTSFORD PLACED OFF GRAVES' TAVERN — 'next door', which is the tightest relative placement in the month. Graves' Tavern is a fixed name in this town and Matthias Mason & Co.'s blacksmith shop is placed off it too (c011 here, and 1834-02-25 c006 which puts the shop 'on Main-street, nearly opposite' it), so the tavern is becoming a survey point with three storefronts hung on it. READ THIS CLAIM TOGETHER WITH 1834-02-25 c001, WHERE THE SAME MAN ADVERTISES FROM THE 'Corner of Dearborn and Lake-sts.' — one tradesman giving two different addresses a week apart is either a move or two premises, and this pass does NOT decide which. The temptation is to conclude that Graves' Tavern stands at Dearborn and Lake, and it is refused: 'next door' and 'corner of' are both Botsford's own frontage, and nothing here says they are the same frontage. Both are recorded and the question goes to the queue.

claims.notes: CHICAGO AS THE END OF A STAGE NETWORK, quoted only where the network touches the town. Two of the nine advertised Illinois lines reach it: Ottawa to Chicago by Holderman's Grove, Walker's Grove and Laughton's, once a week, sixty miles, two and a half days; and a four-horse post coach for Dixon's Ferry and Galena leaving Chicago EVERY THURSDAY. Thursday is the same day the Eastern, Western and Northern mails depart in the postmaster's own timetable (1834-02-11 c002), and the advertisement says why — the Galena coach is timed to make 'a perfect connection with the Detroit mail'. So the town's Thursday morning is its departure morning, on the road and in the post office both, and a reconstruction that wants to know when the streets were busy now has a documented answer. The other seven routes are downstate and are not quoted; the ellipsis is the segmenter's column, not a selection made to flatter the claim.

claims.notes: THE COUNTY'S RECORDS MOVE INTO A NAMED BUILDING, placed off a named house: 'the building one door West of the house of Col. Owen.' Two things follow that the model can use. Col. Owen's HOUSE is a landmark a county officer expects the public to find him by, which puts a dwelling — not a store — among the town's survey points. And the clerk's office is a BUILDING and not a room in the courthouse, one door west of that house, so Cook county's records in February 1834 sit in ordinary town fabric. THE DIRECTION IS TAKEN FROM THIS IMPRESSION AND NOT FROM THE NEXT. The same notice runs at 1834-02-25 (c007 there) where the segmenter renders the same words as 'Rast eat ait', which could be read East; this setting prints 'one door West' cleanly and is the better witness. The discrepancy is recorded rather than smoothed, because west and east of one house are two different lots.

claims.notes: A CORNER PLACEMENT, WHICH IS THE CLASS THAT CAN ACTUALLY PUT A STOREFRONT ON THE GROUND: 'the New Store on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets'. Both streets are platted and the corner is one of four quadrants, so this fixes Kimball to a block face and leaves only the quadrant open — which is as far as the paper goes and as far as this claim goes. The store is called NEW over a November 1833 dateline, so it was built or occupied within about three months of that date, which is a construction window for a South Water Street corner. Kimball is the same storekeeper whose advertisement cut the January letter list to pieces at 1834-01-14 (T-0310 c004); the two readings corroborate each other on the man and the trade. The stock is quoted in full because a dry-goods inventory of that spread implies shelving, counter and window, and the corpus is being read for what buildings contained as well as where they stood.

Peck is the man who reports the town's weekly price current for this paper (1834-02-04 c014), and the two claims explain each other: the storekeeper who quotes the market is the one standing on the corner watching it. claims.notes: THE MANUFACTORY BEHIND THE SMOKE HOUSE. Read with c002 of this issue, Elston's works are one concern with two products and one raw material stream: cash for TALLOW in any quantity and for good HOUSE ASHES — tallow and lye being soap, tallow being candles, and the hogs that render the tallow being the same hogs whose hams go into the smoke house he fitted up on 15 February. That is a documented small industry in a town this project has mostly drawn as stores and dwellings, and it implies a yard, a kettle, ash storage and a smell. The firm signs 'Daniel Elston & Co.' here and 'D. Elston & Co.' in the provision notice; they are recorded as printed and are not merged, which is the identity policy and not an opinion about whether they are the same house.

claims.notes: THE SECOND BLACKSMITH IN THE TOWN AND THE SECOND STOREFRONT HUNG ON GRAVES' TAVERN. This impression loses the preposition — the line reads 've[s]' Tavern' with the offset cut away — and the issue of 1834-02-25 supplies it as 'back on Main-street, nearly [op]posite Graves' Ta[vern]' (c006 there), which is a fuller placement than 'at' and is where the anchor should be taken from. THE SURNAME IS MASON, AND THE '[N]' THIS READING ONCE SUPPLIED IS WITHDRAWN (T-0407). This claim stood with `normalized` reading 'MATTHIAS [N]ASON & CO.' and a business name of 'Matthias Nason & Co.', on a note that said the firm 'is printed NASON here'. It is not: line 2823 of this transcription sets the heading MATTHIAS MASON & CO. whole, on its own line, with no uncertainty marker on it — the interleaved lines of this claim begin two lines below it, at 2825. So there was no unread letter for a bracket to stand in, and the supply contradicted the impression it claimed to read. THE TALLY, by the README's own three greps: nineteen impressions of this standing notice carry the surname's first letter and every one of them is an M — fifteen set MASON whole (1833-12-03, 1833-12-17, 1833-12-24, 1834-02-11, this issue, 1834-03-04, 1834-03-18, 1834-03-25, 1834-06-04, 1834-07-16, 1834-09-24, 1834-10-15, 1834-11-19, 1834-12-03, 1834-12-17), two wreck the S and keep the M (MAJON at 1834-04-08, MADON at 1834-11-26), and two break off at 'MATTHIAS MA' (1834-12-10, 1834-12-24). Not one reads an N. The post office prints the man independently of his own advertisement: 'Mason, Matthias' in the letter lists of 1835-05-20 and 1835-05-27. NOTHING IS AMENDED TO AGREE HERE — the quote is untouched and always read MASON, and what is withdrawn is a reader's supply, not a printing. Together with Pierce & Abbott opposite the Chicago Hotel (1834-02-04 c012), the town supports two forges in February 1834. The Main-street placement the fuller witness gives is not new to the corpus either: T-0310 read this same advertisement at 1834-01-07 (c008 there) as 'on Main-[s]treet, n[early] [o]pposite Grave[s]' Tavern', so February corroborates January rather than adding a street.
